verses.25:21: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink.
verses.25:22: For by doing this you will pile coals of fire on his head, and the Lord will repay you with good things.
verses.25:23: A north wind stirs up clouds, and a shameless face provokes a tongue.
verses.25:24: It is better to live on a corner of a roof than with a reviling woman in a shared house.
verses.25:25: Just as cold water is pleasant to a thirsty soul, so is a good report from a land far away.
verses.25:26: Just as if someone were to block up a spring and ruin an outlet of water, so it is unseemly for a righteous person to have fallen before an ungodly person.
verses.25:27: To eat much honey is not good, but one must honor glorious words.
verses.25:28: Just as a city with its walls torn down and unwalled, so is a man who does anything without counsel.
verses.26:1: Just as dew in harvest and just as rain in summer, so there is no honor for a fool.
verses.26:2: Just as birds and sparrows fly, so an empty curse will not come upon anyone.
verses.26:3: Just as a whip for a horse and a goad for a donkey, so is a rod for a lawless nation.
verses.26:4: Do not answer a fool in line with his folly, so that you do not become like him.
verses.26:5: But answer a fool according to his folly, so that he does not appear wise to himself.
verses.26:6: From his own ways, the one who sends a word through a foolish messenger brings reproach on himself.
verses.26:7: Take away the walking of legs, and lawlessness from the mouth of fools.
verses.26:8: The one who ties up a stone in a sling is like the one who gives glory to a fool.
verses.26:9: Thorns grow in the hand of a drunkard, and slavery in the hand of fools.
verses.26:10: All the flesh of fools is greatly storm-tossed, for their frenzy is crushed.
verses.26:11: Just as a dog, when it goes to its own vomit and becomes detestable, so is a fool who by his own wickedness returns to his own sin. There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace.
verses.26:12: I saw a man who seemed to himself to be wise, yet a fool had more hope than he.
verses.26:13: A sluggard, when sent on the road, says, "A lion is on the roads."
verses.26:14: Just as a door turns on its hinge, so does a sluggard on his bed.
verses.26:15: Having hidden his hand in his bosom, a sluggard will not be able to bring it to his mouth.
verses.26:16: A sluggard appears wiser to himself than the one who brings back a report in fullness.
verses.26:17: Just as the one who takes hold of a dog's tail, so is the one who presides over another's dispute.
verses.26:18: Just as those who heal put forward words to people, and the first one who encounters the word will be tripped up;
verses.26:19: so are all those who lie in ambush for their own friends, and when they are seen, they say, "I was joking when I did it."
verses.26:20: With much wood a fire flourishes, and where there is no double-minded person, a quarrel grows quiet.
verses.26:21: A hearth for coals and wood for fire, and a reviling man is for the turmoil of a quarrel.
verses.26:22: The words of tricksters are soft, yet these strike into the chambers of the inward parts.
verses.26:23: Silver given with deceit must be regarded like a potsherd; smooth lips cover a grievous heart.
verses.26:24: With his lips he agrees to everything while lamenting enemies, but in his heart he devises words.
verses.26:25: If the enemy pleads with you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded; for there are seven evils in his soul.
verses.26:26: The one who conceals enmity contrives deceit, and, being well-known in councils, he covers up his own sins.
verses.26:27: The one who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and the one who rolls a stone rolls it onto himself.
verses.26:28: A false tongue hates truth, and an unguarded mouth causes disturbances.
verses.27:1: Do not boast about the things for tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.
verses.27:2: Let a neighbor praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
verses.27:3: A stone is heavy and sand is hard to carry, but the anger of a fool is heavier than both.
verses.27:4: Wrath is merciless and anger is sharp, but jealousy tolerates no one.
verses.27:5: Open reproofs are better than hidden friendship.
verses.27:6: The wounds of a friend are more trustworthy than the willing kisses of an enemy.
verses.27:7: A soul that is full scoffs at honeycombs, but to a soul in need even bitter things seem sweet.
verses.27:8: Just as when a bird flies down from its own nest, so a man is enslaved when he is estranged from his own places.
verses.27:9: A heart is delighted by perfumes and wines and incense, but a soul is torn apart by misfortunes.
verses.27:10: Do not forsake your friend or a friend of your father, and do not enter into the house of your brother when you suffer misfortune; better is a friend nearby than a brother living far away.
verses.27:11: Become wise, son, so that your heart may be glad, and turn away reproachful words from yourself.
verses.27:12: A shrewd man hides himself when evils approach, but fools press on and will pay the penalty.
verses.27:13: Take away his garment, for he has passed by; whoever ruins what belongs to others is an insolent man.
verses.27:14: Whoever blesses a friend early in the morning with a loud voice will seem no different from one who curses.
verses.27:15: Drops drive a man out of the house on a wintry day; likewise also a reviling woman out of his own house.
verses.27:16: The north wind is a harsh wind, yet by name it is called favorable.
verses.27:17: Iron sharpens iron, and a man sharpens the face of a companion.
verses.27:18: He who plants a fig tree will eat its fruits, and he who guards his own master will be honored.
verses.27:19: Just as faces are not like faces, so neither are the minds of people.
verses.27:20: Hades and destruction are not filled; likewise also the eyes of people are insatiable. An abomination to the Lord is one who fixes his eye, and the undisciplined are unrestrained in tongue.
verses.27:21: A test for silver and gold is smelting, and a man is tested through the mouth of those who praise him. The heart of a lawless man seeks out evils, but an upright heart seeks knowledge.
verses.27:22: If you flog a fool in the midst of a council, dishonoring him, you will by no means remove his folly.
verses.27:23: You shall thoroughly know the lives of your flock, and you shall set your heart on your herds;
verses.27:24: for a man does not have power and strength forever, nor does he hand them down from generation to generation.
verses.27:25: Care for the green plants in the field, and you will cut grass, and gather mountain hay,
verses.27:26: so that you may have sheep for clothing; value a field, so that you may have lambs.
verses.27:27: Son, from me you have strong sayings for your life and for the life of your servants.
verses.28:1: An ungodly man flees when no one pursues, but a righteous man is confident like a lion.
verses.28:2: Because of the sins of the ungodly, disputes arise, but a shrewd man will quench them.
verses.28:3: A man bold in ungodly acts extorts from the poor. Just as a violent and unprofitable rain,
verses.28:4: so those who forsake the law praise ungodliness; but those who love the law surround themselves with a wall.
verses.28:5: Evil men will not understand judgment, but those who seek the Lord will understand in everything.
verses.28:6: Better is a poor man who walks in truth than a false rich man.
verses.28:7: An understanding son keeps the law, but he who shepherds debauchery dishonors his father.
verses.28:8: He who multiplies his wealth with interest and excessive gains gathers it for the one who shows mercy to the poor.
verses.28:9: He who turns away his ear so as not to listen to the law, he himself has made his prayer abominable.
verses.28:10: He who leads the upright astray on an evil way will himself fall into ruin, and the lawless will pass by good things and will not enter into them.
verses.28:11: A rich man is wise in his own estimation, but a discerning poor man will condemn him.
verses.28:12: Because of the help of the righteous great glory comes about, but in the places of the ungodly people are caught.
verses.28:13: He who covers over his own ungodliness will not prosper, but he who declares reproofs will be loved.
verses.28:14: Blessed is the man who shrinks back from everything out of reverence, but he who is hard of heart will fall into evils.
verses.28:15: A hungry lion and a thirsty wolf is one who, being poor, tyrannizes a needy nation.
verses.28:16: A king lacking revenues is a great extortioner, but he who hates injustice will live a long time.
verses.28:17: He who goes surety for a man under a charge of murder will be a fugitive and not in safety. Discipline a son and he will love you, and he will give adornment to your soul; you shall by no means obey a lawless nation.
verses.28:18: He who walks righteously has been helped, but he who walks in crooked ways will be entangled.
verses.28:19: He who works his own land will be filled with bread, but he who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty.
verses.28:20: A trustworthy man will be greatly blessed, but the evil man will not go unpunished.
verses.28:21: He who does not respect the faces of the righteous is not good; such a one will sell a man for a morsel of bread.
verses.28:22: An envious man hurries to become rich, and he does not know that a merciful man will prevail over him.
verses.28:23: He who reproves a person's ways will have favors more than the one who flatters with his tongue.
verses.28:24: He who rejects father or mother and thinks he is not sinning, this one is a partner of an ungodly man.
verses.28:25: An unbelieving man judges rashly, but he who trusts in the Lord will be cared for.
verses.28:26: He who trusts in a rash heart, such a one is a fool; but he who walks in wisdom will be saved.
verses.28:27: He who gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who turns away his eye will be in great distress.
verses.28:28: In the places of the ungodly the righteous groan, but at their destruction the righteous will be multiplied.
verses.29:1: Better is a man who reproves than a stiff-necked man, for when he is suddenly burned, there is no healing.
verses.29:2: When the righteous are praised, peoples will rejoice, but when the ungodly rule, men groan.
verses.29:3: The father of a man who loves wisdom rejoices, but the one who shepherds prostitutes will lose wealth.
verses.29:4: A righteous king raises up a land, but a lawless man tears it down.
verses.29:5: Whoever prepares a net before the face of his own friend casts it around his own feet.
verses.29:6: For a man who sins there is a great snare, but a righteous man will be in joy and in gladness.
verses.29:7: A righteous man knows how to judge for the needy, but the ungodly man does not understand knowledge, and a poor man does not have a discerning mind.
verses.29:8: Lawless men set a city ablaze, but the wise turn away wrath.
verses.29:9: A wise man judges nations, but a worthless man, when he becomes angry, is laughed at and does not cower.
verses.29:10: Men who share in bloodshed hate a devout man, but the upright will seek out his soul.
verses.29:11: A fool brings out all his anger, but a wise man dispenses it bit by bit.
verses.29:12: When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless.
verses.29:13: When a lender and a debtor meet one another, the Lord exercises oversight over both.
verses.29:14: When a king judges the poor in truth, his throne will be established for a testimony.
verses.29:15: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a child who goes astray puts his parents to shame.
verses.29:16: When the ungodly are many, sins become many, but when those people fall, the righteous become greatly afraid.
verses.29:17: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest, and he will give adornment to your soul.
verses.29:18: There will by no means be an interpreter for a lawless nation, but the one who keeps the law is blessed.
verses.29:19: A stubborn servant will not be disciplined by words; for even if he understands, yet he will not obey.
verses.29:20: If you see a man hasty in words, know that a fool has more hope than he does.
verses.29:21: Whoever lives in luxury from childhood will be a servant, and in the end he will grieve over himself.
verses.29:22: A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, and an angry man digs up sins.
verses.29:23: Arrogance humbles a man, but the Lord supports the humble-minded with glory.
verses.29:24: Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul; and if, when an oath is put forth, they hear it and do not report it,
verses.29:25: fearing and feeling shame before people, they are tripped up; but the one who trusts in the Lord will rejoice. Ungodliness brings a fall to a man, but whoever trusts in the Master will be saved.
verses.29:26: Many court the favor of rulers, but justice for a man comes from the Lord.
verses.29:27: A righteous man is an abomination to an unjust man, and a way that goes straight is an abomination to a lawless man.
verses.30:1: Fear my words, son, and having received them, repent. These things the man says to those who believe in God, and I cease.
verses.30:2: For I am the most foolish of all people, and the understanding of people is not in me.
verses.30:3: God has taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of the holy ones.
verses.30:4: Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered winds in his bosom? Who has wrapped up water in a garment? Who has taken hold of the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is the name of his children?
verses.30:5: For all the words of God are refined by fire, and He Himself shields those who revere Him.
verses.30:6: Do not add to His words, so that He may not reprove you and you may not become a liar.
verses.30:7: Two things I ask from You; do not take away grace from me before I die:
verses.30:8: Put a vain and false word far from me, and do not give me wealth or poverty, but appoint for me what is necessary and what is sufficient,
verses.30:9: so that, being filled, I may not become a liar and say, "Who sees me?" or, becoming poor, steal and swear by the name of God.
verses.30:10: Do not hand over a servant into the hands of a master, or he may curse you and you will be destroyed.
verses.30:11: An evil offspring curses its father, and does not bless its mother.
verses.30:12: An evil offspring judges itself righteous, yet has not washed away its discharge.
verses.30:13: An evil offspring has lofty eyes, and lifts itself up with its eyelids.
verses.30:14: An evil offspring has swords for its teeth and knives for its molars, so as to consume and devour the humble from the earth and their needy from among people.
verses.30:15: The leech had three daughters loved with love, and these three did not satisfy her. And the fourth was not content to say, "Enough":
verses.30:16: Hades, and the passion of a woman, and Tartarus, and earth not satisfied with water, and water, and fire will never say, "It is enough."
verses.30:17: An eye that mocks a father and dishonors the old age of a mother, may ravens from the ravines peck it out, and may the young of eagles devour it.
verses.30:18: Now there are three things impossible for me to understand, and the fourth I do not comprehend:
verses.30:19: the tracks of a flying eagle, and the ways of a serpent on a rock, and the paths of a ship sailing the sea, and the ways of a man in youth.
verses.30:20: Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, when she acts, washes herself and says she has done nothing wrong.
verses.30:21: Because of three things the earth is shaken, and the fourth it cannot bear:
verses.30:22: if a servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food,
verses.30:23: and if a female servant drives out her own mistress, and if a hated woman obtains a good husband.
verses.30:24: Now there are four very small things on the earth, yet these are wiser than the wise:
verses.30:25: the ants, which have no strength, yet prepare their food in summer;
verses.30:26: and the rock badgers, a people not strong, who make their own homes in the rocks;
verses.30:27: the locust is without a king, yet marches out in good order at a single command;
verses.30:28: and a gecko, supporting itself with its hands and easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of kings.
verses.30:29: Now there are three things that walk steadily, and a fourth that strides well:
verses.30:30: a lion's cub, stronger than beasts, which does not turn back nor cower before any beast;
verses.30:31: and a high-spirited rooster walking about among hens, and a male goat leading a herd of goats; and a king speaking publicly in a nation.
verses.30:32: If you give yourself over in gladness, and stretch out your hand with quarreling, you will be dishonored.
verses.30:33: Draw milk, and there will be butter; and if you squeeze nostrils, blood will come out; and if you draw out words, judgments and quarrels will come out.
verses.31:1: My words have been spoken by God; an oracle of a king whom his mother instructed.
verses.31:2: What, child, will you keep? What? Sayings of God. Firstborn, I speak to you, son. What, child of my womb? What, child of my vows?
verses.31:3: Do not give your wealth to women, nor your mind and life to regret.
verses.31:4: Do all things with counsel; drink wine with counsel. Rulers are hot-tempered, and let them not drink wine,
verses.31:5: so that by drinking they may not forget wisdom and be completely unable to judge the weak rightly.
verses.31:6: Give strong drink to those in sorrow, and wine to drink to those in anguish,
verses.31:7: so that they may forget their poverty and no longer remember their troubles.
verses.31:8: Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all soundly.
verses.31:9: Open your mouth and judge justly, and decide the case of the poor and the weak.
verses.31:10: Who will find a valiant woman? And such a one is more precious than costly stones.
verses.31:11: The heart of her husband has confidence in her; such a one will not lack fine spoils.
verses.31:12: For she works good things for her husband all her life.
verses.31:13: Spinning wool and flax, she made something useful with her hands.
verses.31:14: She became like a ship trading from afar; and she herself gathers her livelihood,
verses.31:15: and rises while it is still night. And she gave food to her household and tasks to her maidservants.
verses.31:16: Having inspected a field, she bought it, and from the fruits of her hands she planted a property.
verses.31:17: Having girded her waist strongly, she set her arms firmly to work.
verses.31:18: And she tasted that it is good to work, and her lamp is not extinguished the whole night.
verses.31:19: She stretches out her forearms to profitable things, and she sets her hands firmly to the spindle.
verses.31:20: And she opened her hands to the poor, and stretched out her wrist to the destitute.
verses.31:21: Her husband does not worry about those in the house whenever he lingers somewhere, for all those with her are clothed.
verses.31:22: She made double cloaks for her husband, and garments of fine linen and purple for herself.
verses.31:23: And her husband becomes distinguished at the gates whenever he sits in council with the elders, inhabitants of the land.
verses.31:24: She made and sold linen garments, and sashes to the Canaanites. She opened her mouth carefully and lawfully, and established order for her tongue.
verses.31:25: She clothed herself with strength and splendor, and rejoiced in the last days.
verses.31:26: The ways of her houses are closely kept, and she did not eat the food of idleness.
verses.31:27: And she opens her mouth to the wise in accordance with law, and her mercy
verses.31:28: raised up her children and they became rich, and her husband praised her:
verses.31:29: "Many daughters have acquired wealth, many have done mighty things; but you stand above and have surpassed them all."
verses.31:30: Charms are false, and a woman's beauty is vain; for a discerning woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord.
verses.31:31: Give her from the fruits of her lips, and let her husband be praised at the gates.

notes.1:3: Greek στροφὰς λόγων ("turns of words") refers to intricate, subtle, or artfully turned expressions.
notes.1:7: The Greek text reads "fear of God" rather than "fear of the Lord" and contains an expanded double couplet echoing Psalm 110:10 LXX (111:10 MT).
notes.1:17: Verse 1:16 is absent from this Greek text, which proceeds directly from 1:15 to 1:17; the Greek reads ἀδίκως ("unjustly") where the Hebrew reads "in vain."
notes.1:22: The Septuagint diverges markedly from the Hebrew here, opening with a conditional promise for the innocent ("As long as...") rather than a rebuke of the simple.
notes.1:32: Greek νηπίους ("infants") can also mean "the naive," and ἐξετασμός ("scrutiny") denotes judicial examination or inquiry.
notes.2:2: The Septuagint treats verse 2 as the future consequence of verse 1 and includes an additional third clause regarding the admonition of one's son.
notes.2:16: Here and through verse 19 the Septuagint warns against "evil counsel" (κακὴ βουλή) rather than the Hebrew's "strange" or "forbidden woman."
notes.2:18: Greek γηγενῶν ("earthborn") renders the Hebrew Rephaim (shades of the dead or primeval giants), and ἄξονας ("courses") literally means tracks or axles.
notes.2:20: The Septuagint casts this verse as a contrary-to-fact conditional ("For if they had walked... they would have found...") rather than a purpose clause.
notes.3:6: The Greek uses the feminine pronoun "her" (αὐτήν), referring to wisdom rather than masculine "Him" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and the verb ὀρθοτομέω literally means "cut straight."
notes.3:12: The Greek reads "flogs" (μαστιγοῖ), a reading reflected in Hebrews 12:6, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "as a father [the son in whom he delights]."
notes.3:15: The Septuagint includes two additional clauses in verse 15 ("nothing evil will oppose her. She is well known to all who draw near to her") and an additional couplet in verse 16 ("righteousness goes forth from her mouth, and she bears law and mercy upon her tongue") not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.3:18: The Greek renders the second clause "and to those who lean upon her as upon the Lord," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "and those who hold her fast are called blessed."
notes.3:32: Following the primary Septuagint witnesses, the Greek text includes the negation "not" (οὐ), making the lawless person the subject who does not sit in council among the righteous, rather than God having intimacy with the upright as in the Hebrew.
notes.4:4: The Greek uses plural verbs ("who spoke and taught me") and "our word," presenting both the father and the mother as speakers of the instruction in verses 4-9.
notes.4:6: Because the Greek text lacks the opening clause of verse 5 and all of verse 7 found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the feminine pronouns in verses 6-9 grammatically look back to "utterance" (ῥῆσιν) in verse 5 while continuing the personification of wisdom.
notes.4:21: Reading the Hebrew term for "eye/spring" as "spring," the Greek has "your springs" (αἱ πηγαί σου) rather than "your eyes."
notes.4:27: The Septuagint concludes chapter 4 with an extended addition contrasting the ways on the right and on the left and promising that God will make paths straight, which has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.5:2: Greek reads 'and the perception of my lips commands you' (compare MT 'and that your lips may guard knowledge'), and 5:3 opens with the LXX-distinct warning 'Do not pay attention to a worthless woman.'
notes.5:16: Unlike MT's rhetorical question, the Greek draws a contrast between forbidding waters to overflow from one's spring and directing one's waters to pass through into one's own streets.
notes.5:19: Greek paraphrases the marital imagery compared to MT and uses the rare adjective pollostos ('very great' or 'greatly multiplied'), likely reflecting Hebrew sg' ('grow great') and playing on polys ('much') in 5:20.
notes.5:23: Greek reads 'dies with the undisciplined' (compare MT 'for lack of discipline') and adds that he 'was cast out from the abundance of his own life.'
notes.6:3: Greek isthi here is the imperative of 'be' with a participle (literally 'be not growing faint'); in 6:6 the same form stands for ithi ('Go').
notes.6:8: The Greek text contains an extended comparison to the bee (from 'Or go to the bee' to the end of the verse) not found in MT, as well as an additional couplet on diligence in 6:11.
notes.6:16: Instead of MT's numerical saying ('six things... seven'), the Greek connects this verse directly to the wicked man of 6:12-15 ('because he rejoices in all things that God hates, and he is crushed because of impurity of soul').
notes.6:22: After the plural 'laws' and 'ordinances' of 6:20-21, the Greek shifts abruptly to a feminine singular pronoun (auten, here 'it'), echoing the Hebrew singular antecedent and anticipating 'commandment' in 6:23; in 6:23, 'and a light' could alternatively be construed as the predicate of 'the way of life.'
notes.6:26: The genitive andron ('of men') stands between 'woman' and 'precious souls' and can alternatively be construed with 'woman' ('a wife/woman of men ensnares precious souls'), echoing MT's 'a man's wife.'
notes.7:1: The second sentence ("Son, honor the Lord...") is a Septuagint-distinctive expansion not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:6: Unlike the Hebrew (where the narrator looks through his own window), the Greek depicts the woman herself peering from her house, and 7:8 uniquely describes the young man as speaking in the passages of her houses.
notes.7:22: Greek κεπφωθείς ("lured on") is a rare verb derived from κέπφος, a gullible seabird easily lured into a trap. The Greek also distinctively compares the youth to a dog led to bonds and, in 7:23, a stag struck in the liver by an arrow.
notes.7:27: Greek ᾅδου ("Hades") is the Septuagint rendering for the realm of the dead (corresponding to Hebrew Sheol).
notes.8:1: Unlike the Hebrew rhetorical question ("Does not wisdom call?"), the Greek addresses the reader directly with a second-person statement.
notes.8:21: The second sentence ("If I declare to you...") is a Septuagint-distinctive transition into Wisdom's creation discourse; verse 8:33 is absent in the Greek text.
notes.8:22: Greek ἔκτισεν means "created" (whereas the corresponding Hebrew verb can also mean "acquired/possessed"), and in 8:25 Greek γεννᾷ ("brings forth") notably uses the present tense.
notes.8:30: Greek ἁρμόζουσα means "fitting things together" (as an artisan) or "being in harmony." In 8:31, the masculine participle συντελέσας makes the Lord, rather than Wisdom, the one rejoicing after completing the inhabited world.
notes.8:35: Greek ἔξοδοι ("exits" or "ways out") mirrors "entrances" in 8:34 and reflects reading the underlying Hebrew root as "go out" rather than "find."
notes.9:6: The Greek reads "reign forever" (βασιλεύσητε) and adds "and seek prudence," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "live" without the additional clause.
notes.9:10: The Greek reads "counsel of holy ones" (βουλὴ ἁγίων) and includes the third clause about knowing the law, which is not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.9:12: The verb rendered "endure" (ἀντλήσεις) literally means "draw" or "bail out," an idiom for suffering hardship; the extended saying from "Whoever leans on falsehoods" onward is a distinctive Septuagint expansion.
notes.9:16: Unlike 9:4 ("she said"), the Greek shifts to the first person ("I urge, saying," παρακελεύομαι λέγουσα), placing the entire verse in the direct speech of the foolish woman.
notes.9:18: Greek γηγενεῖς ("the earthborn") renders the Hebrew Rephaim (shades of the dead), and πέτευρον ("plank") can denote a perch or trap-board; the admonition from "Instead, leap away" to the end is an extended Septuagint passage.
notes.10:4: The second sentence ("A disciplined son will be wise...") is a Septuagint addition not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.10:10: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text repeats the warning of 10:8b, the Greek reads "the one who reproves with openness makes peace" (μετὰ παρρησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ).
notes.10:13: The Greek text here contains only this clause continuing from 10:12 (other witnesses and the Hebrew include an opening line about wisdom on the lips); "senseless" literally renders ἀκάρδιον ("without heart").
notes.10:18: The Greek reads "Righteous lips cover hostility" (χείλη δίκαια), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of lying lips concealing hatred.
notes.11:3: The Greek text differs markedly from the Hebrew MT here (and omits verse 4). 'Regret' (μετάμελον) refers to the sorrow left among the living at a righteous person's death, while 'swift' (πρόχειρος) literally means 'ready at hand.'
notes.11:10: In the Greek text, verses 10 and 11 form a single couplet, omitting the second half of verse 10 and the first half of verse 11 found in the Hebrew MT.
notes.11:15: The phrase 'sound of security' (ἦχον ἀσφαλείας) reflects the distinctive Greek reading, contrasting with the Hebrew MT's reference to those who strike hands in pledge.
notes.11:25: The Greek clause ψυχὴ εὐλογουμένη πᾶσα ἁπλῆ ('Every blessed soul is sincere') may also be construed 'Every sincere soul is blessed.'
notes.11:31: This Greek rendering—differing from the Hebrew MT's 'repaid on the earth'—is quoted verbatim in 1 Peter 4:18.
notes.12:11: The second couplet is a Septuagint addition absent from the Hebrew MT; 'delights in lingering over wine' literally reads 'is pleasant in wine-pastimes' (ἡδὺς ἐν οἴνων διατριβαῖς).
notes.12:13: The second couplet is a Septuagint addition absent from the Hebrew MT; 'looks gently' literally translates the Greek idiom βλέπων λεῖα ('looking smooth things').
notes.12:18: The Greek text prints the nominative plural μάχαιραι ('swords'), taken metaphorically in apposition to the speakers ('like swords'); some Greek manuscripts read the dative singular μαχαίρᾳ ('with a sword').
notes.12:23: The Greek reads 'throne of discernment' (θρόνος αἰσθήσεως), reflecting a Hebrew consonantal reading for 'throne' rather than the MT's 'conceals.'
notes.12:26: The rare Greek word ἐπιγνώμων can function either as an adjective ('fair-minded / discerning') modifying 'righteous person' or as a noun ('a righteous arbiter').
notes.13:5: Verse 13:6 is absent from the Greek Septuagint text, so the verse numbering moves directly from 13:5 to 13:7.
notes.13:9: The second sentence is an additional couplet preserved in the Greek Septuagint that is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (similar expansions appear in 13:11 and 13:13).
notes.13:12: The Greek text differs markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('Hope deferred makes the heart sick...'), contrasting sincere help for beginners with mere promises that raise hopes.
notes.13:17: The Greek reads 'king' (basileus) in the first clause rather than the Hebrew 'messenger,' contrasting a reckless king with the wise messenger who rescues him.
notes.14:10: The Greek expression 'sensitive heart' (kardia aisthetike, recurring in 14:30) reflects a distinctive Septuagint reading linking heightened sensitivity with sorrow, and 'arrogance' (hybris) stands where the Hebrew reads 'stranger.'
notes.14:15: The Greek reads 'comes to repentance' (metanoia, also meaning 'change of mind' or 'reconsideration'), differing from the Hebrew ('considers his steps').
notes.14:22: The Greek text contains a four-line proverb built on artisan wordplay (tektaino 'craft' and tekton 'craftsman'), expanding the two-line Hebrew proverb.
notes.14:26: The unexpressed subject of 'leaves behind' and the pronoun 'his' are ambiguous in Greek; they may refer to the God-fearing person, to the Lord Himself ('He'/'His'), or to the fear of the Lord ('it').
notes.14:32: The Greek reads 'in his own holiness' (hosiotes), reflecting a different textual reading from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('in his death').
notes.15:1: The Greek opens with an additional clause ("Anger destroys even the prudent") absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and uses the participle hypopiptousa, literally "yielding" or "submissive," for the answer that turns away wrath.
notes.15:5: πανουργότερος ('more shrewd') is used here in a positive sense. The second half of this verse and verse 6 give two parallel sayings on the strength of the righteous and the ruin of the ungodly.
notes.15:23: The Greek continues verse 22 directly, referring back to "counsel" with "it" and stating that the evil person will say nothing timely and good for the public community (to koino).
notes.15:27: In the Septuagint, verses 27-29 incorporate sayings corresponding to Masoretic 16:6-9, which accounts for the shorter verse sequence at the opening of chapter 16 in the Greek text.
notes.15:33: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("before honor is humility"), the Greek reads "the beginning of glory will answer it," referring back to wisdom or discipline.
notes.16:15: The Greek reads "a king's son" (huios basileos) rather than the Masoretic "a king's face," and "a late cloud" (nephos opsimon) refers to the clouds bringing the welcome late spring rains.
notes.16:16: The Greek literally reads nossiai ("nests"), reflecting an Old Greek rendering distinct from the Masoretic "getting" or "acquiring."
notes.16:21: Rather than stating that the wise of heart will be called discerning, the Greek states that people call the wise and discerning "worthless" (phaulous), contrasting them with those sweet in speech who "will hear more."
notes.16:26: The verb ekbiazetai ("forces away") sets up a direct contrast with the following clause ("yet"), opposing the hardworking man who staves off ruin to the crooked man who bears destruction on his own mouth.
notes.16:33: Unlike the Masoretic Text's reference to casting the lot into the lap, the Greek makes no mention of lots, contrasting all things that come into the laps of the unrighteous with all righteous things coming from the Lord.
notes.17:3: The Greek reads "hearts are chosen in the sight of the Lord" (ἐκλεκταὶ καρδίαι παρὰ Κυρίῳ), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Lord tests hearts."
notes.17:6: The second sentence is unique to the Septuagint; an "obol" (ὀβολός) was a small Greek coin of minimal value.
notes.17:8: The Greek reads "discipline" (παιδεία) where the Hebrew has "a bribe"; the singular verbs in the second clause may refer either to discipline itself or to the one who uses it.
notes.17:12: The Greek differs sharply from the Hebrew ("Let a bear robbed of her cubs meet a man..."), reading "Anxiety will fall upon a discerning man."
notes.17:19: In the Septuagint, material parallel to Hebrew 17:19b appears at the end of 17:16, causing the verse boundaries across 17:19–21 to divide sentences mid-clause.
notes.18:8: The Greek differs completely from the Hebrew ("The words of a whisperer..."), closely paralleling Greek Proverbs 19:15; "the effeminate" (ἀνδρογύνων) denotes soft, unmanly, or timid persons.
notes.18:9: The Greek reads "does not heal himself" (μὴ ἰώμενος αὐτόν), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew root rendered "is slack" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.18:10: The Greek reads "from greatness of strength" (ἐκ μεγαλωσύνης ἰσχύος) rather than the Hebrew "a strong tower," and the dative pronoun αὐτῷ ("to it") may refer either to the name of the Lord or directly to the Lord ("to Him").
notes.18:18: The Greek reads "a silent person" (σιγηρός) where the Hebrew reads "the lot."
notes.18:22: The second half of this verse ("the one who casts out...") is an addition in the Septuagint, which concludes chapter 18 here without the equivalent of Hebrew 18:23–24.
notes.19:6: The Septuagint reads 'every evil person becomes a reproach to a man' (apparently reading Hebrew ra', 'evil,' rather than rea', 'friend'), where the Masoretic Text has 'everyone is a friend to a giver of gifts.'
notes.19:7: The Septuagint includes two additional proverbial couplets in this verse ('Good insight...' and 'The one who does much evil...') that do not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.19:11: The Greek 'his boast comes upon lawbreakers' reflects a literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom 'his glory is to pass over transgression.'
notes.19:13: In the second clause the Septuagint reads 'vows from the wages of a prostitute are not pure' (cf. Deut 23:18), diverging from the Hebrew 'a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping.'
notes.19:23: The Septuagint's 'where knowledge is not attended to' reflects reading a Hebrew form meaning 'knowledge' rather than 'evil/harm' as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.20:6: Greek 'a human being is a great thing' renders Hebrew 'many a man' literally; 'a hard task' translates the Greek idiom ergon with an infinitive.
notes.20:9: In the Septuagint, the three sayings corresponding to Hebrew 20:20-22 are placed immediately after 20:9, while Hebrew 20:14-19 are absent from the Greek text.
notes.20:11: The Greek syntax and punctuation are difficult; following the critical text's punctuation, 'the one who makes them' is the subject of 'will be tripped up,' though other editions attach that phrase to verse 10 and take 'a young man with a devout person' as the subject.
notes.20:27: The Greek masculine singular relative pronoun ('who') specifically identifies the Lord as the one who searches the inner chambers, whereas the Hebrew phrasing can refer to the breath or lamp.
notes.21:7: The Greek verb epixenothesetai literally means "will lodge as a guest with," reflecting a Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew verb as "sojourn" rather than "sweep away."
notes.21:9: The Septuagint reads "in whitewashed rooms with unrighteousness" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "with a quarrelsome woman."
notes.21:16: Greek giganton ("giants") is the standard Septuagint rendering of Hebrew Rephaim ("shades" or "the dead").
notes.21:18: Greek perikatharma ("expiation") literally denotes a ritual cleansing or expiatory offering, used here to render Hebrew "ransom."
notes.21:30: The Septuagint reads "courage" and "for the ungodly," diverging notably from the Masoretic Text ("understanding" and "against the Lord").
notes.22:7: The Greek active verb daniousin literally means "will lend," reversing the sense of the Masoretic Text ("the borrower is the slave of the lender").
notes.22:8: The second sentence ("God blesses a cheerful man and a giver...") is a Septuagint addition absent from the Masoretic Text and echoed in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
notes.22:15: Greek paidia is an ancient spelling of paideia ("discipline"); unlike the Masoretic Text ("drives it far from him"), the Septuagint states that a rod and discipline "are far from him."
notes.22:23: Greek rhuse sen asulon psuchen ("you will rescue your inviolable soul") diverges sharply from the Masoretic Text ("will despoil of life those who despoil them").
notes.22:29: The Septuagint renders the opening Hebrew verb ("Do you see?") as the adjective horatikon ("observant") and reads nothrois ("sluggish") instead of the Masoretic Text's "obscure."
notes.23:5: The Greek reads οὐδαμοῦ πεσεῖται ("it will fall nowhere," where some manuscripts read φανεῖται, "will appear") and refers to τοῦ προεστηκότος αὐτοῦ ("the one set over him"), which may denote a patron or master, or metaphorically God.
notes.23:22: Verse 23:23 of the Hebrew text is not present in the Greek Septuagint tradition, so numbering proceeds directly from 23:22 to 23:24.
notes.23:27: The Greek uses the classical image of a "perforated jar" (πίθος τετρημένος) and speaks of a "foreign house" (ἀλλότριος οἶκος) and "narrow foreign well" (φρέαρ στενὸν ἀλλότριον), differing markedly from the Hebrew.
notes.23:31: The expression "more naked than a pestle" (γυμνότερος ὑπέρου) is an ancient Greek proverb describing total destitution.
notes.24:5: The Greek reads "a large farm" (γεωργίου μεγάλου), differing from the Hebrew phrasing about increasing strength.
notes.24:9: The Greek syntax of 24:9-10 is difficult, with "impurity" (ἀκαθαρσία) in the nominative as the subject of the passive verb ἐμμολυνθήσεται ("will be stained into") alongside "a pestilent man" (ἀνδρὶ λοιμῷ).
notes.24:22: The Greek contains an extended section on royal speech and wrath not found in the Hebrew; in "A son who guards a word will be free from destruction," the genitive "destruction" (ἀπωλείας) is governed by "free from" (ἐκτός), not by "son."
notes.24:27: The Greek reads "walk behind me" (πορεύου κατόπισθέν μου), reflecting a different reading from the Hebrew "and afterward."
notes.24:31: The masculine pronouns ("him," "he," "his") can refer either to the foolish person of 24:30 under the extended vineyard metaphor or to the vineyard itself; χορτομανήσει vividly means "run wild with weeds."
notes.25:1: Greek hai adiakritoi literally means 'the undistinguished' or 'the unseparated,' often understood as 'unarranged' or 'obscure,' and has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text. The Greek also reads 'friends' (a royal court title) rather than 'men' and 'Judea' rather than 'Judah.'
notes.25:12: The Greek syntax is compact, literally reading 'is fastened for a golden earring and a precious sardius, a wise word to an attentive ear,' using a predicative construction to equate a wise word with precious adornment.
notes.25:13: The Greek reads exodos ('a going out,' 'exit,' or 'outlet,' compare 25:26) rather than 'snow' as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.25:20: The Greek diverges substantially from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, pairing the comparison of vinegar on a wound with a second saying about a moth in a garment and a worm in wood.
notes.26:7: The Greek uses a second-person imperative ('Take away') and reads 'lawlessness' rather than 'a proverb,' presenting a markedly different saying from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:11: The second sentence ('There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace') is a Septuagint addition shared verbatim with Sirach 4:21.
notes.26:16: The Greek reads en plesmone ('in fullness' or 'in satiety'), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text's 'seven.'
notes.26:18: The Greek reads hoi iomenoi ('those who heal') and logous ('words'), differing sharply from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's image of a madman throwing firebrands and arrows.
notes.26:26: The Greek source text reads enkalyptei ('covers up') rather than the variant ekkalyptei ('uncovers'), portraying the deceitful person as trying to conceal his sins even though he is well-known in councils.
notes.27:4: In the Greek text, jealousy (zelos) is the grammatical subject of hyphistatai with oudena ('no one') as its direct object, literally 'jealousy bears with/tolerates no one,' rather than the Hebrew question 'who can stand before jealousy?'
notes.27:11: The Greek text reads second-person pronouns ('your heart' and 'from yourself') rather than the first-person pronouns found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:16: The Greek presents an ironic saying about the north wind, rendering the Hebrew term for 'right hand' with epidexios ('on the right, auspicious, favorable').
notes.27:20: Both verses 20 and 21 contain an additional Septuagint couplet not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:27: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text mentions goats' milk as food for the household, the Septuagint closes the chapter with a didactic statement about 'strong sayings' for life.
notes.28:3: In the Greek syntax, the simile at the end of verse 3 ('Just as a violent and unprofitable rain') directly introduces the main clause at the start of verse 4 ('so those who forsake the law...').
notes.28:9: The Greek uses the transitive perfect middle ebdelyktai with autos as subject and ten proseuchen autou as direct object, meaning 'he himself has made his prayer abominable.'
notes.28:15: The Septuagint refers to a 'thirsty wolf' and a tyrant who is 'poor' (ptochos on), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'rushing bear' and 'wicked ruler.'
notes.28:17: In addition to its distinct first couplet about going surety for one charged with murder, the Septuagint includes a second couplet on disciplining a son and refusing to obey a lawless nation.
notes.28:22: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text warns that 'want' or 'poverty' will come upon the envious man, the Septuagint reads eleemon ('a merciful man'), reflecting a different underlying Hebrew reading.
notes.29:1: Greek frames this as a comparison ("Better is a man who reproves than a stiff-necked man") and uses the verb meaning "burned" or "inflamed," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "broken."
notes.29:7: The third clause ("and a poor man does not have a discerning mind") is distinctive to the Septuagint, likely arising from a double rendering in which Hebrew rasha' ("wicked") was read as rash ("poor").
notes.29:14: Greek "for a testimony" (eis martyrion) reflects reading the Hebrew consonantal text as "for a witness/testimony" rather than "forever."
notes.29:16: Greek "become greatly afraid" reflects reading the Hebrew verb as "fear" rather than "see."
notes.29:25: The opening clause completes the conditional sentence begun in 29:24, and the Septuagint preserves a double rendering of the verse using both Kyrios ("the Lord") and despotes ("the Master").
notes.30:1: The Septuagint translates the Hebrew heading's proper names (Agur, Jakeh, Ithiel, and Ucal) as common words and verbs, producing an exhortation to a son and the closing words "and I cease."
notes.30:3: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I have not learned wisdom"), the Greek states affirmatively, "God has taught me wisdom."
notes.30:12: Greek exodos (literally "going out, issue, discharge") renders Hebrew tso'ah ("filth/excrement") via an etymological or euphemistic link to "going out."
notes.30:16: The Septuagint expands the list with Tartarus (the Greek name for the underworld abyss) alongside Hades, and includes both "water" and "fire."
notes.30:19: Greek "in youth" (en neoteti) reflects reading the Hebrew consonantal text as "in youth" rather than "with a young woman."
notes.31:1: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which names King Lemuel, the Greek text reads 'My words have been spoken by God,' rendering the Hebrew consonants as a reference to God.
notes.31:20: Greek karpon here translates the anatomical term for 'wrist' in parallel with 'hands' in the first clause, though the identical Greek form can also mean 'fruit.'
notes.31:24: Greek reads 'to the Canaanites' (τοῖς Χαναναίοις), a proper name where the Hebrew has the word for 'merchant'; in this Greek text the verse also includes her opening her mouth carefully and lawfully.
notes.31:27: The sentence runs across verses 27-28 in the Greek ('her mercy raised up her children'), and this Greek clause about opening her mouth to the wise has no counterpart in the Hebrew text.
notes.31:31: The Greek text reads 'fruits of her lips' (rather than 'hands') and closes with 'let her husband be praised at the gates' (rather than 'let her works praise her').
